draft.title: Liquidity ratio
card: Liquidity is a business's ability to pay its short-term debts when they fall due. The current ratio is one way to measure it.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. Current assets are cash and items that will soon become cash. Current liabilities are debts due within a year.
A ratio of 2 to 1 means the business has $2 of current assets for every $1 of current liabilities. Around 2 to 1 is often seen as healthy.
A ratio well below 1 to 1 can signal trouble paying debts on time. A very high ratio may mean cash or stock is sitting idle instead of being put to use.
draft.remember: The current ratio compares what a business can turn into cash soon with what it must pay soon.

a.q: A business has current assets of $60 000 and current liabilities of $40 000. What is its current ratio?
opts: 2 to 1
a.why: Current ratio = $60 000 ÷ $40 000 = 1.5, so 1.5 to 1. The tempting answer 0.67 to 1 comes from dividing the wrong way round, with liabilities on top.
a.clue: Current assets go on top of the division.

b.q: Priya's bakery in Orange has current assets of $18 000 and current liabilities of $36 000. What does its current ratio suggest?
opts: It may struggle to pay its short-term debts
It can easily pay its short-term debts
It relies heavily on borrowed money
It makes a low profit on each sale
b.why: The ratio is $18 000 ÷ $36 000 = 0.5 to 1, so the bakery has only 50 cents of current assets for each $1 of current liabilities. That is well below 1 to 1 and points to trouble paying debts on time. The current ratio does not measure borrowing or profit, so the last two options are wrong.
b.clue: Work out the ratio, then compare it with 1 to 1.

b.best: It may struggle to pay its short-term debts

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'). The others are flat claims ('relies heavily', 'can easily', 'makes a low profit'), so a student could pick it without working out the ratio. Hedging some of the distractors would fix this.

Why (b) says 'the last two options are wrong', but the options appear in random order. In the order shown, the borrowing and profit options are first and third, so the explanation points to the wrong options. Name the options instead.
